Elliot Glazer mentioned the follows in a tweet:

PFIRS has the same consistency strength as Lean, and the same local consequences, but can generalize those results to global theorems

This isn't a conclusion seen in any paper as far as I know. It's a well known result that Lean's type theory, with the classical axioms, is equi-interpretable with ZFC+{there exists n inaccessible cardinals | n is a natural number}. In the discussion thread, Glazer appeared to show that this equi-interpretability doesn't mean the two systems have the same global consequences.

Does anyone have any idea about why Lean and ZFC+PFIRS have the same global consequences?
If you search here for “pfirs” you can find explainations. Maybe we can collect all the links in one place.
Here is a good one: https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/621470-lean4lean/topic/Set.20theoretic.20model/with/614077114

It appears the relevant proof is given in this post:
https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/621470-lean4lean/topic/Set.20theoretic.20model/near/614077114

The Lean => ZFC+PFIRS part appears straightforward. I have a more explicit version of the proof (but I'm not sure about its correctness as I'm not formally trained in metamathematics):

Notation:

  • σ\sigmaσ: a set theoretic statement, i.e. a sentence in the set theoretic language L∈\mathcal{L}_\inL∈​
  • σVκ\sigma^{V_\kappa}σVκ​: relativization of σ\sigmaσ in VκV_\kappaVκ​. That's to say, ∀x\forall x∀x in σ\sigmaσ is replaced by ∀x(x∈Vκ→⋯ )\forall x (x \in V_\kappa \to \cdots)∀x(x∈Vκ​→⋯), and ∃x\exist x∃x in σ\sigmaσ is replaced by ∃x(x∈Vκ∧⋯ )\exist x (x \in V_\kappa \land \cdots)∃x(x∈Vκ​∧⋯).
  • σ^n\hat{\sigma}_nσ^n​: the Lean statement that σ\sigmaσ holds in universe nnn. That's to say, a Lean statement obtained by replacing ∀x\forall x∀x in σ\sigmaσ by ∀x:ZFSet{n}\forall x : \mathtt{ZFSet}\{n\}∀x:ZFSet{n} and replacing ∃x\exist x∃x in σ\sigmaσ by ∃x:ZFSet{n}\exist x : \mathtt{ZFSet}\{n\}∃x:ZFSet{n}.

Suppose for some nnn, Lean⊢σ^0∨⋯∨σ^n−1\mathsf{Lean} \vdash \hat{\sigma}_0 \lor \cdots \lor \hat{\sigma}_{n-1}Lean⊢σ^0​∨⋯∨σ^n−1​. The proof may use far more universes than nnn but by virtue of being of a finite length, there has to be an upper bound - say NNN - of the number of universes used (as Lean doesn't allow quantifying over universes).

That's to say, Lean⊢σ^0∨⋯∨σ^n−1\mathsf{Lean} \vdash \hat{\sigma}_0 \lor \cdots \lor \hat{\sigma}_{n-1}Lean⊢σ^0​∨⋯∨σ^n−1​ is provable in the subtheory of Lean, Leanσ\mathsf{Lean}_\sigmaLeanσ​, that contains finite universes. Suppose towards contraction that the theory T=ZFC+PFIRS+¬σT = \mathsf{ZFC} + \mathsf{PFIRS} + \lnot \sigmaT=ZFC+PFIRS+¬σ is consistent.

We now start building a proof along the following procedure in TTT. Applying PFIRS, in ZFC+PFIRS we have ∃λ0(Inacc(λ0)∧(¬σ)Vλ0)\exists \lambda_0 (\mathrm{Inacc}(\lambda_0) \land (\lnot \sigma)^{V_{\lambda_0}})∃λ0​(Inacc(λ0​)∧(¬σ)Vλ0​​). Now applying PFIRS to ¬σ∧∃λ0(Inacc(λ0)∧(¬σ)Vλ0)\lnot \sigma \land \exists \lambda_0 (\mathrm{Inacc}(\lambda_0) \land (\lnot \sigma)^{V_{\lambda_0}})¬σ∧∃λ0​(Inacc(λ0​)∧(¬σ)Vλ0​​) we get ∃λ1(Inacc(λ1)∧(¬σ)Vκ1∧∃λ0(λ0∈Vλ1∧Inacc(λ0)∧σVλ0))\exist \lambda_1 (\mathrm{Inacc}(\lambda_1) \land (\lnot \sigma)^{V_{\kappa_1}} \land \exist \lambda_0 (\lambda_0 \in V_{\lambda_1} \land \mathrm{Inacc}(\lambda_0) \land \sigma^{V_{\lambda_0}}))∃λ1​(Inacc(λ1​)∧(¬σ)Vκ1​​∧∃λ0​(λ0​∈Vλ1​​∧Inacc(λ0​)∧σVλ0​​)). We can repeat this process over and over again, and this means that for an arbitrary mmm, we have ∃λ0∃λ1⋯∃λm(λ0∈Vλ1∧λ1∈Vλ2∧⋯∧λm−1∈Vλm∧(¬σ)Vλ0∧(¬σ)Vλ1∧⋯∧(¬σ)Vλm)\exist \lambda_0 \exist \lambda_1 \cdots \exist \lambda_m (\lambda_0 \in V_{\lambda_1} \land \lambda_1 \in V_{\lambda_2} \land \cdots \land \lambda_{m-1} \in V_{\lambda_m} \land (\lnot \sigma)^{V_{\lambda_0}} \land (\lnot \sigma)^{V_{\lambda_1}} \land \cdots \land (\lnot \sigma)^{V_{\lambda_m}})∃λ0​∃λ1​⋯∃λm​(λ0​∈Vλ1​​∧λ1​∈Vλ2​​∧⋯∧λm−1​∈Vλm​​∧(¬σ)Vλ0​​∧(¬σ)Vλ1​​∧⋯∧(¬σ)Vλm​​).

This means that in ZFC+PFIRS, we can find a finite chain κ0<κ1<⋯<κN−1\kappa_0 < \kappa_1 < \cdots < \kappa_{N-1}κ0​<κ1​<⋯<κN−1​ such that for every i<Ni < Ni<N, (¬σ)Vκi(\lnot \sigma)^{V_{\kappa_i}}(¬σ)Vκi​​, where NNN can be arbitrarily big. ("Repeating this process over and over again" means induction in the metalanguage and not in ZFC+PFIRS: we are performing induction over proofs in ZFC+PFIRS). Now, by the standard correspondence between Lean with finitely many universes and ZFC+finitely many inaccessible cardinals, a model of TTT is also a model of Leanσ\mathsf{Lean}_\sigmaLeanσ​ - and yet in such a model σ\sigmaσ holds in no Lean universe. Contradiction. Thus TTT cannot be consistent and thus ZFC+PFIRS⊢σ\mathsf{ZFC} + \mathsf{PFIRS} \vdash \sigmaZFC+PFIRS⊢σ.

On the other hand, I don't see the idea behind the ZFC+PRIFS=> Lean part of the proof. It appears to be a pigeonhole argument but I don't see why a PFIRS instance can only fail at most once in the set theoretic universes in Lean.

There is also another issue if we want to interpret this correspondence as some sort of equivalence between Lean and set theoretic foundations of mathematics. The statement σ\sigmaσ in the equivalence theorem is a set theoretic one. Is it possible to prove that "ordinary" or "idiomatic" formalized mathematics in Lean can all more or less recast into statements about ZFSet?

@Elliot Glazer for questions about the proof.

As for other interpretations you can do higher order arithmetic (even further from Lean but at least clear numbers mean the intended thing), ETCS statements inside Set with universes (inside ZFC like theories), and I bet you can also do HOL plus choice and universes (but that is harder for mathematicians to appreciate). I bet the last two could cover many lean features with less encoding.

Jason Rute said:

As for other interpretations you can do higher order arithmetic (even further from Lean but at least clear numbers mean the intended thing), ETCS statements inside Set with universes (inside ZFC like theories), and I bet you can also do HOL plus choice and universes (but that is harder for mathematicians to appreciate). I bet the last two could cover many lean features with less encoding.

Regarding the question whether set theoretic equivalence between Lean and ZFC+PFIRS can be generalized to a generic equivalence result between expressiveness of Lean and ZFC+PFIRS, maybe we can show that every piece of formalized mathematics in Lean using a finite number of type theoretic universes can be translated to a formalization using only ZFSet? So you have the following equivalence relations: idiomatic Lean <=> ZFSet heavy Lean <=> ZFC+PFIRS

I think lean-inductive-models (@Joachim Breitner) already has a translation of (most?/all?) inductives to a few basic Lean types and then those can be translated (maybe in an ugly way) to ZFSet set theory.
I guess unlike lean-inductive-models (which just uses this translation as an interpretation of Lean), you would want to also prove it is faithful (which would be good for Lean metatheoretically).

Jason Rute said:

which would be good for Lean metatheoretically

One side remark: I think it would be beneficial if we can have all discussions on the metatheoretic properties of Lean in a centralized section of Lean's documentation. It should for example cover the interpretation between Lean and ZFC+{there are n inaccessible cardinals | n is a natural number}, the set theoretic correspondence between Lean and ZFC+PFIRS, and the aforementioned inductive types-to-ZFSet embedding.

Eventually people will ask what kind of mathematics Lean is capable of formalizing and whether fundamental changes of mind from the "old" set theoretic foundations of mathematics are needed if one wants to work in Lean. It's a good idea to keep the relevant information in a single place.

Does a formal statement of some equivalence here actually represent the informal idea that ordinary mathematics in Lean corresponds to ordinary mathematics in ZFC? Most of the math being formalized in Lean is not being expressed in finite-order arithmetic or ZFSet, and thus wouldn't be covered by these statements.

[Don't get me wrong, I still think it's an interesting question...]

Cameron Zwarich said:

Does a formal statement of some equivalence here actually represent the informal idea that ordinary mathematics in Lean corresponds to ordinary mathematics in ZFC? Most of the math being formalized in Lean is not being expressed in finite-order arithmetic or ZFSet, and thus wouldn't be covered by these statements.

This is precisely why I asked "The statement σ\sigmaσ in the equivalence theorem is a set theoretic one. Is it possible to prove that "ordinary" or "idiomatic" formalized mathematics in Lean can all more or less recast into statements about ZFSet?"

I think ultimately these questions should be asked because eventually people will ask if the transition to Lean involves anything fundamentally different from the post-1930s understanding of the foundation of mathematics.

I think there are a number of translations of inductives to zfc:

  1. We can use the lean-inductive-models translation to translate inductives to simple types and those to ZFC.
  2. We could use the recursion theorem of ZFC to define the equivalent of inductives.
  3. We could justify inductives as the unique types/sets up to equivalence satisfying the recursors. Then show the ZFC translation works for any translation of inductives to ZFC which satisfies this property (including the two above).

This is all a bit vague but I think we could translate Lean to categorical set theory where lean’s constructors are given by universal properties. Then one could work in that setting (like ETCS with universes), or translate again to ZFC language.

I think all of those things work (although your condition in 3 will probably not be much more than a restatement of some least fixed point property), but the resulting definitions in ZFC probably won't be the definitions used in ordinary mathematics, so you still have a semantic gap. I guess you could pick individual definitions and show that enough specific definitions like smooth manifolds, schemes, von Neumann algebras, etc. define equivalent categories between the two?

My view of definitions used in normal mathematics is that almost all of them can be characterized as “the unique X with property P up to equivalence E”. The only way to do it is to align these definitions one by one, but it is not like mathematicians even do this in practice. It’s probably enough to do for a few complicated but standard objects (say smooth manifolds), and leave the rest as an exercise to the reader.
Or at least this isn’t a Lean issue. This is a formalization issue. Even formalizing in ZFC directly would have this alignment issue with normal mathematics.

FWIW I'm not convinced that most mathematical definitions are characterised by a universal property (other than some kind of tautological universal property saying e.g. "the unique definition which is this definition"). What is the universal property for groups or topological spaces, for example? It might be closer to being true for constructions within theories but I'm not sure it's true for theories themselves.

@Kevin Buzzard I think “Groups” are a great example. The class of groups (say on small sets) can be characterized as maps Groups : Type 0 -> Type 0 and mul : (G : Groups X) -> G -> G -> G which satisfies a few axioms (the usual group ones) and are universal in that given another such Group’ and mul’ satisfying those axioms you can map those “groups” into homeomorphic objects in Group. All such univeral maps are “equivalent” (in that you can map objects from one to homeeomophic objects in the other). Yes I’m basically saying what it means to be the equivalent Lean structure (with the Lean recusors), but this way one doesn’t have to use the same fields and are free to define a group with or without explicit units or inverses—or group exponents like in Mathlib’s Group. One can also use non structure definitions of “groups” like invertable monoids , groupoids with one element, automorphisms of first order structures, subgroups of a permutation group, etc. The key is that from every one of these definitions you can construct the corresponding Group and mul maps.l, show they satisfy the axioms, and they are universal.

I think similarly you can describe the category of groups as the unique Functor from Set to a category G such that … (but I haven’t worked it out).

OK so then this is problematic, because you're telling me that the universal property of groups is [write down the axioms of a group], so then what is the universal property of perfectoid spaces, given that it took us 18000 lines of code to define them in Lean 3? We say the universal property is "write down the 18000 lines again" and this cannot tell us anything useful.

I guess Im not saying every definition has a short univeral property. Certainly some, like reals, have a characterization which is shorter than the usual construction, but not all. I’m more saying that there are general techniques to align definitions of the same objects between seperate developments or even between logics. I don’t know how easy it is in practice to use them, but at least some of this could be automated from the existing definitions, but of course, domain knowledge may tell you a shorter characterization.

(I don’t know about petfectoid spaces. I asked Gemini which is giving me some options but you are the expert so I won’t pretend I know anything here. I did think a lot of your 18000 lines were showing perfectoid spaces existed, and if so you don’t need existence in your characterization, just like you can describe the reals uniquely without constructing them. But maybe I am mistaken about the repo.)

I’m more saying that there are general techniques to align definitions of the same objects between seperate developments

And I'm arguing against this claim in general (although I agree that it is true in many cases). I think that for the kind of complex mathematical objects which are kicking around in my personal area of expertise, which is a very "cathedral"-like area consisting of definitions building on definitions building on definitions, one can make different design decisions and then proving that two definitions of an object coincide may be an extremely deep theorem. To give a concrete example: our definition of perfectoid space did not coincide with Scholze's, we took a short cut at some point and gave a definition which was mathematically equivalent to Scholze's, but the proof that the definitions were equivalent was 30 pages of valuation theory which we never formalized (and is still not formalized, although Tau Ceti is moving towards it).

Yes, I agree. I don’t mean to make this sound easy, just possible. By “general”, I mean the gluing theorems often have a general form, not that the gluing theorems are always easy to prove (especially if the two defintions are objectively quite different).
Universal properties aren't universal if you change your foundations!

Once you get into category theory and consider things like the category of groups, you need to introduce small/large distinctions via universes or some other mechanism, and it's even less obvious that the same concepts formalized with different expressions of the small/large distinction are actually the "same" thing.

MacLane was bothered by this problem and hoped that some form of categorical foundations would eliminate it, but there are a number of results that show the inevitability of the large/small distinction if you want the mathematics that we're used to.

I've discussed this idea with @James E Hanson and @Mario Carneiro before. One issue is there are questions stateable in but independent of Lean (+ 3 standard axioms) that prevent full translation into the ZFSet type, such as:

  1. Type comparison issues like "is N=Z?"
  2. Questions regarding the choices made by the global choice function, like "is the chosen real number positive?"
  3. Size ambiguities of the set-theoretic heights of the universes, like "Does the first universe type correspond to the first inaccessible cardinal?"

I could suspect these 3 ambiguities could be filled in respectively via:

  1. Some axiom that systematically rejects nonprovable equalities of types (Mario suggests to me this might be better-behaved than the opposite disambiguation: trying to declare the type-theoretic universe behaves like the cardinality model),
  2. Replace Classical.choice with the conjunction of Classical.axiomOfChoice and unique choice,
  3. It might be possible to demand the universes be consecutive inaccessibles, but I'm less sure about that. The way universe-indexing works in Lean is still confusing to me. (Also, rather than demanding the first universe be at the first inaccessible, I think it would be preferable to demand the first universe be either the first inaccessible or some limit-ordinal-indexed inaccessible, to avoid deriving anti-large cardinal results. This would lead to better translation properties between this extension of Lean vs ZFC).

This concept of a foundational system not having "inessential independence" is actually a precise concept actively being studied by logicians. So a precise objective I'd like to achieve is finding a Lean axiomatization that is solid in the sense defined here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1702.07093

there are basically no constraints on the mapping of lean universes to inaccessibles, any strictly increasing map will do. You can take the first omega if you want, or skip over inaccessible number 37 if you like, or have a countable number of universes between every universe

Is the assertion "for all n, the nth universe is the nth inaccessible" expressible by a single axiom?

Edit: Astra proposes the following:

axiom consecutiveUniverses.{u} :
    (∀ κ : Cardinal.{0}, ¬ κ.IsInaccessible) ∧
    (∀ κ : Cardinal.{u + 1},
      κ.IsInaccessible → κ ≤ Cardinal.univ.{u, u + 1})

@Elliot Glazer that depends a bit on what you mean by a single axiom. Top-level axiom definitions (like other definitions) in Lean are more like an axiom schema parameterized by universes. You couldn't express the quantification over all universes as the consequence of a theorem (but you could prove a theorem that is itself parameterized by a universe).

I hadn't fully appreciated that even the standard axioms are schemas. Is the fact that applying print axioms to Mathlib-acceptable proofs just results in 3 axioms the result of dropping universe parameters? Like could it have been set up that e.g. Classical.choice.{u} got separately tracked for each u that arises in a proof?

Edit: alright I see this seems to be why the equivalence of ϕ\phiϕ in ZFC+PFIRS is ⋁uZFSet.{u}⊨ϕ\bigvee_{u} \mathsf{ZFSet}.\{u\} \vDash \phi⋁u​ZFSet.{u}⊨ϕ: we are essentially applying the pigeonhole argument in Lean and a priori it's not possible to know what ZFSet.{u} exactly satisfies ϕ\phiϕ.

Just to make sure I (and perhaps other non-metamathematicians here) understand everything. So the logic is essentially this:

  1. We want a proof theoretic translation between Lean and set theoretic foundations, because the existing translations are model theoretic and don't allow us to bring statements back and forth between foundations (which turns a statement phi into something like f(g(phi))).
  2. But to have such a translation we have to take every Lean statement seriously. In particular, certain questions in Lean have well-defined set theoretic counterparts that are provable or refutable and yet are independent of Lean.
  3. To get this done one can add new axioms to Lean to make questions that are supposed to be ask answerable.
  4. Am I right to say that this enriched version of Lean is supposed to be a strict superset (when it comes to provable statements) of the current [Lean + classicla axioms]? If so, then we have proven that all formalized mathematics in the current version of Lean has well-defined set theoretic counterparts.
  5. This translation won't necessarily produce conventional set theoretic formalization of mathematics (for instance, natural numbers aren't necessarily going to be defined in the usual von Neumann encoding) but this is ultimately a problem of doing formalization purely within set theories and proving that different encodings are equivalent.

Am I understanding everything correctly?

Is the fact that applying print axioms to Mathlib-acceptable proofs just results in 3 axioms the result of dropping universe parameters? Like could it have been set up that e.g. Classical.choice.{u} got separately tracked for each u that arises in a proof?

Following this line, do we know what a theorem schema (with universe parameters) in Lean looks like once translated to set theoretic foundations? For example what does "ϕ\phiϕ holds in ZFSet.{u}, u being a universe parameter" translate to in ZFC+PFIRS? Sure, it means ϕ\phiϕ holds in ZFC+PFIRS, but this is not a bidirectional translation: we then can only translate this theorem in ZFC+PFIRS back to Lean as "in a certain ZFSet, ϕ\phiϕ holds", with the existing equivalence theorems.
